passage: The colony's Saturday football match in Dwarka was short one player, and Anand, captain as usual, looked over the boys by the gate. The new boy from B-block spoke slow Hindi with a Malayalam accent and carried a physics book. "He'll be useless," Anand muttered to Disha. "Nerd type." He picked a tall boy with spiky hair instead, who looked like he played. Disha rolled her eyes and put the new boy on her team. In twenty minutes the new boy had scored twice, weaving past Anand as if he wasn't there. The tall boy missed three easy passes. At half-time Anand walked over, red-faced. "Where did you learn to play like that?" "School team, back home in Kozhikode," the boy said.

qa.q: How many goals did the new boy score in twenty minutes?
qa.a: The new boy scored twice in twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Anand feel sure the new boy would be useless?
qa.a: The accent and the physics book matched Anand's idea of a nerd type, and the tall spiky-haired boy looked like a player, so the match to a type felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Anand try as captain next time?
qa.a: He could ask new players what they play and watch a few minutes of passing before choosing, instead of picking by looks or accent.

qa.q: How might the new boy have felt when Anand called him useless?
qa.a: If he heard it, he may have felt dismissed and eager to prove himself, and scoring twice probably felt satisfying.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging a new boy's football skill from his accent and a physics book, and being surprised by the game.

passage:
"That new boy in tuition has an earring and ripped jeans," Pradeep said, reaching for the rice. "He's obviously the trouble type."
"Obviously?" his cousin Chaitanya asked. "Did he do anything?"
"No, but you can tell. And the girl who sits in front, the one who talks so softly? Topper. Definitely."
"Based on?"
"Based on... she has neat handwriting."
Mausi laughed from the kitchen. "And what did the test say?"
Pradeep went quiet. "The earring guy got the highest marks. The soft-spoken girl failed."
"So?" Chaitanya grinned.
"So... it was a weird test," Pradeep said, but he was frowning into his plate.
"Or," said Chaitanya, "maybe you can't tell."

qa.q: What did the test show about the boy with the earring?
qa.a: The earring guy got the highest marks.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep call it a weird test?
qa.a: Pradeep feels uncomfortable because the results clash with the types he had in his head, and blaming the test lets him keep those guesses. His frown suggests he half suspects he was wrong.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do the next time he forms a quick judgment about a classmate?
qa.a: He could ask himself what he has actually seen the person do, and wait for real evidence, like marks or behaviour, before labelling them.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya keep asking short questions instead of lecturing?
qa.a: Chaitanya seems to want Pradeep to notice the gap himself; questions like "Based on?" let the facts do the arguing without starting a fight.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy deciding who is trouble and who is a topper from looks and voice, then being surprised when the test disagrees.

passage: When I was in class nine, I thought I could read people like a scoreboard. My name is Pranav, and I was the kid who sorted everyone in the first week. Vidya was small, wore thick glasses and spoke so softly that the teacher kept asking her to repeat. So in my head she went into a box: bookish, bad at sports. When we were put in the same relay team for sports day, I groaned out loud. Then in practice she ran the third leg and overtook two runners. It turned out she had been training for district athletics since she was ten. I remember standing there with the baton, feeling stupid. I'd been so sure. It had felt exactly like knowing.

qa.q: Which leg of the relay did Vidya run?
qa.a: Vidya ran the third leg and overtook two runners.

qa.q: Why did Pranav groan when put in Vidya's relay team?
qa.a: Her small size, thick glasses and soft voice fitted Pranav's box of bookish and bad at sports, so the guess felt like knowing.

qa.q: What could Pranav tell a younger student who sorts people in the first week?
qa.a: That a first-week guess from looks or voice is only a guess; wait to see what people actually do, like how they run in practice, before deciding.

qa.q: How might Vidya have felt hearing Pranav groan?
qa.a: Vidya may have felt hurt or underestimated, and perhaps quietly determined to show what she could do in practice.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging a classmate as bad at sports from her size, glasses and soft voice, and being surprised by the relay.

passage:
Teacher's note: Class 9 chemistry, practical lab, 12 August. Written by Nikita Sharma.
Today I let students pick lab partners for the titration practical. Gautam, usually thoughtful, avoided Birsa, the tall boy who joined on the sports quota. I heard Gautam tell his friend, "He's a footballer, he won't know titration." He chose the student with the neatest notebook instead. During the practical, Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times. Birsa and his partner got a clean result on the first try, and Birsa explained the colour change to the next table. Gautam watched with his mouth half open. After class he came to my desk and said, "Ma'am, I thought he'd be bad at this. I was wrong." We talked about how he had decided before seeing any evidence. Next week I'll rotate partners at random, and I've asked Gautam to work with Birsa.

qa.q: What happened to Gautam's pair during the practical?
qa.a: Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times.

qa.q: Why did it seem sensible to Gautam that Birsa wouldn't know titration?
qa.a: Gautam felt confident because Birsa was tall and joined on the sports quota, which fit his idea of a footballer, not a chemist. The match to a type felt like enough reason.

qa.q: What did Nikita decide to do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: She will rotate partners at random and has asked Gautam to work with Birsa, so Gautam can learn about Birsa from real work instead of assumptions.

qa.q: What might it be like for Birsa to be overlooked as a lab partner?
qa.a: Birsa may be used to people assuming sports is all he is good at, and explaining the colour change to the next table may have felt like a quiet way of proving otherwise.

grounding: A teacher notes that a teenage boy avoided a sports-quota classmate as a lab partner, assuming he'd be weak, and was surprised by his skill.

passage:
Friday, 9 pm
Diary, I owe someone an apology, but only in here.
The new girl, Indu, joined our class last week. She has heavy kajal, loud bangles, and she talks back to teachers in a way that makes everyone gasp. So on day one I told Ronit, "Trouble. You'll see. She'll be in the principal's office in a month." And every time she laughed in class I thought, see?
Today I lost my wallet in the canteen. It had my bus pass and the fifty rupees Papa gave me. I was panicking. Then Indu came up and handed it to me. "Found it under the bench. Count it." Everything was there.
I just stood there like a fool and said thanks. I had her figured out completely wrong, and I didn't even know her.
Mummy says a good son says sorry properly. Maybe Monday.
Vaibhav

qa.q: What was in Vaibhav's wallet?
qa.a: His bus pass and the fifty rupees Papa gave him.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel sure that Indu was trouble?
qa.a: Her kajal, bangles and way of talking back matched his idea of a troublemaker, so every laugh in class seemed to confirm it.

qa.q: What choice is Vaibhav thinking about for Monday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Saying sorry properly to Indu. It would mean acting on what he learned from what she did, not on his first judgement.

qa.q: How might Indu feel if she knew Vaibhav had called her trouble on day one?
qa.a: She might feel hurt or unsurprised, if people often judge her by her look, and his apology could mean a lot to her.

grounding: A teenage boy's diary shows he judged a new girl as trouble from her looks and speech, and was surprised when she returned his lost wallet.
